extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/logic; readers interested in epistemology and the theory of induction and deduction
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length critique and exposition on the nature and limits of deductive and inductive reasoning, examining the status of axioms, the hypothetical character of deduction, and the claim that inconceivability of a negation is the ultimate test of truth. It addresses how assumptions, experience, and modes of conception bear on belief and certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of mathematical certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical certainty (unconditional truth and perfect accuracy) is not an attribute of all mathematical truths but only of those that relate to pure Number as distinct from Quantity, and only so long as numbers are not taken as a precise index to actual quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: arithmetic propositions about number alone are exact; conclusions that infer equality of other properties from numerical equality (e.g., pounds of different standards, horse power equivalence) introduce hypothetical elements. Geometry and mechanics offer certainty of inference under suppositions, but not certainty that the suppositions exactly hold in reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive sciences are hypothetical
rubrics_metrics.description: All deductive sciences proceed by tracing consequences of certain assumptions and are therefore hypothetical; the truth or approximate truth of those assumptions must be examined separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proper method is to determine the inferences that follow from assumptions (which can be done in general) and to leave to separate empirical inquiry the question of how true or closely approximated the assumptions are in each particular case. Demonstrative science consists in pre-computing consequences so they are ready when particular cases arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the truth/approximation of premises empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: When deduction starts from premises that are not exact (i.e., outside pure number), part of the inquiry must determine how much the premises lack exact truth for the case at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This evaluation is generally a matter of observation repeated in each case; if argument must be used instead of observation, different evidence may be required in different cases. One should not conflate certainty of inference with certainty of premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of reductio ad absurdum
rubrics_metrics.description: Reductio ad absurdum (deriving contradiction to show falsity) is an allowable and useful method for showing that an assumption leads to absurd consequences and thus must be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is effective for demonstrating the falsity of premises by showing contradiction, but it cannot force assent from someone who denies the validity of the ratiocination itself; the method rests on accepting the reasoning process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivability of a proposition's negation is not a definitive test of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that the inability to conceive the negation of a proposition establishes its truth (Spencer's doctrine) is critiqued: inconceivability may not reflect genuine evidence and therefore is not a reliable ultimate test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections include that inconceivability can result from mistaken suppositions about experience, tradition, or associative habits of thought; it can misrepresent actual experience. Even where inconceivability corresponds to uniform experience, the uniformity itself is the proper evidence and should be stated directly rather than inferred via inconceivability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of experience is the substantial evidence for belief
rubrics_metrics.description: If a belief is grounded in the perfect agreement of past experience, that uniformity (not merely inconceivableness of the negation) is the real evidence entitling the belief to acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity varies in strength as evidence: some uniformities pervade nature and provide strong grounds (e.g., causal regularities), while others are weak and liable to counterexample (e.g., 'all swans are white' prior to discovering Australia). When possible, state and weigh the uniformity of experience directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish two senses of 'inconceivable' (idea vs belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconceivability has a double meaning: (a) inability to form an idea (unimaginable), and (b) inability to accept or hold a belief (unbelievable). These must not be conflated in argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antipodes are imaginable (an idea can be formed) but were historically unbelievable; trying to conceive an end to space may be genuinely unimaginable. Clarify which sense is intended when invoking inconceivability as a test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate momentary conception with enduring belief
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that a person at a moment cannot rid their mind of an idea (or cannot, in a particular context, conceive the negation) does not prove that they permanently believe it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish transient, situational impressions (e.g., fears invoking belief in ghosts in a dark place) from the permanent state of belief. When claiming a belief is 'invariable', verify its persistence across contexts and over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated use of the same axiom does not multiply error-chances
rubrics_metrics.description: In multi-step reasoning, repeatedly invoking the same true axiom does not create multiple independent chances of error; if the axiom is true, its repetition does not weaken the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An argument's reliability is threatened only if new, uncertain premises are introduced at intermediate steps. Thus, the number of deductive steps alone does not necessarily make reasoning less secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of non-evidential causes of inconceivability (association/tradition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconceivability can arise from causes unrelated to experiential evidence, such as tradition, strong associative habits, or familiar modes of explanation, and so may mislead when used as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples include the Cartesian insistence on contact for motion and the habitual conception of sunrise as the sun's motion. Investigate whether alleged inconceivability stems from such psychological causes rather than from the absence of countervailing experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Widespread belief is a fact requiring explanation, not automatic proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A general or apparently spontaneous belief (e.g., in an external material world) is a psychological phenomenon that must be explained; its prevalence does not by itself prove its objective truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents of a widely held belief may accept the challenge to explain its origin if not by the thing's objective existence. Do not treat ubiquity of belief as conclusive evidence without examining alternative psychological origins.
